https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: New South Wales recorded its first cases of H5 bird flu in two local birds on Saturday, including one found near Wentworth on the Murray-Darling Basin. Jack Gough, chief executive of the Invasive Species Council, said: That should be ringing alarm bells for governments because it suggests it could soon be spreading among inland bird colonies ahead of spring breeding season. Birds in the Murray-Darling basin are already in decline due to feral animals, insufficient water to critical wetlands and the loss of habitat - now they have a deadly disease to contend with. Samples from two deceased greater crested terns in NSW – the other found near Narooma on the south coast – tested positive at CSIRO’s Australian Centre for Disease Preparedness. On Saturday, a further 28 positive cases were confirmed in South Australia, bringing the state’s total to 147. An additional 13 suspected cases were also detected, including an ibis in Adelaide and a cormorant in Carpenter Rocks on the Limestone Coast.

http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/27/911-t.text: A US military judge has set a 5 June 2028 trial date for Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and three others accused of plotting the 11 September 2001 attacks.Mohammed was considered one of Al-Qaeda leader Osama bin Laden's top lieutenants before he was captured in March 2003 in Pakistan.The date is 18 months later than prosecutors requested, allowing more time to resolve pretrial disputes, including over what evidence can be presented.US authorities have spent more than two decades trying to bring the case to trial. The 2028 date could still be delayed if pretrial deadlines are not met. A previous trial scheduled for 2021 was cancelled.Mohammed is accused of developing and directing the plot to hijack passenger planes and crash them into the World Trade Center and the Pentagon. A fourth hijacked plane crashed into a field in Pennsylvania. The attacks killed nearly 3,000 people.The failed plea dealMohammed faces trial alongside three alleged accomplices - Walid bin Attash, Ali Abdul Aziz Ali and Mustafa al-Hawsawi - who are accused of helping organise or facilitate the attacks.A federal appeals court last year rejected a plea deal that would have allowed Mohammed to plead guilty and avoid the possibility of execution.The agreement would have given Mohammed and two co-defendants life sentences without parole and required them to answer questions from victims’ families. The Biden administration later rejected the deal after two years of negotiations.A key legal issue has been whether the defendants can receive a fair trial after being tortured in CIA custody. The plea deal would have avoided some of those disputes.Mohammed and his three alleged accomplices are among the last detainees held at the US military base at Guantanamo Bay, Cuba.The facility held roughly 800 prisoners at its peak, but they have since slowly been sent to other countries. A small fraction of that number remain.

https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/14/saud.text: Saudi Arabia is relying on stored oil to maintain exports after drone attacks shut its East-West pipeline, threatening deliveries to buyers in Europe and Asia.Saudi Arabia’s energy ministry announced the shutdown on Friday as a precaution, after the pipeline was attacked in the Riyadh and Medina regions last Thursday.It said emergency and technical teams were securing the pipeline and checking its safety.Saudi and Iraqi authorities said the drone attack originated in Iraq. The ministry’s announcement did not say when pumping would resume or give a full account of the damage.Saudi oil buyers and traders quoted in reports published on Sunday estimated that a prolonged shutdown could put at risk around 4 million barrels a day, or about 4% of global oil supply.They estimated that oil stored at the Red Sea port of Yanbu could keep exports going for five to seven days. Saudi authorities have not confirmed either estimate.The effect on deliveries will depend on how quickly pumping resumes and how much stored oil is available.Brent crude futures rose around 3% in early trading on Monday following further attacks on energy facilities and shipping in the Middle East.A route around HormuzThe roughly 1,200km pipeline carries oil from eastern Saudi Arabia to Yanbu on the west coast. It allows exports to leave through the Red Sea without tankers passing through the Strait of Hormuz.Aramco said in May that it had increased pumping through the pipeline to its maximum capacity of 7 million barrels a day during the first quarter, helping maintain exports while shipping through Hormuz was disrupted.The pipeline also supplies refineries on Saudi Arabia’s west coast, so its capacity is not the same as the amount exported.The shutdown does not mean global oil supplies immediately fall by 7 million barrels a day. Tankers can still load oil stored near export terminals, but those supplies will run down unless more oil arrives.Deliveries to Europe and AsiaFrom Yanbu, tankers heading to Europe can sail north through the Red Sea towards the Suez Canal and the Mediterranean. Egypt’s SUMED pipeline offers another route, carrying oil between the Red Sea and Mediterranean coasts.The direct sea route to Asia runs south through Bab el-Mandeb, the narrow passage between the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden, and then towards the Indian Ocean.That route faces a separate threat from Yemen’s Houthis, who have seized Perim Island in the passage and the country's Red Sea coast, effectively taking control of the strait.Tankers heading to Asia could instead sail north through Suez and then around Africa, but the journey would be much longer. Changing a tanker’s route does not solve the problem of getting oil to Yanbu.The International Energy Agency said in its September oil market report that stored oil supplies worldwide had fallen by 507 million barrels since February, including 95 million barrels in August alone.The agency estimated Gulf oil exports at around 13 million barrels a day in August, nearly half their pre-war level. It also reported sharply higher diesel prices in Europe and Asia as disruptions reduced fuel supplies.

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: A man has been convicted and fined $10,000 after the discovery of hundreds of taxidermied and frozen native animals at a property in Kyneton. Photograph: Conservation Regulator Victoria View image in fullscreen A man has been convicted and fined $10,000 after the discovery of hundreds of taxidermied and frozen native animals at a property in Kyneton. Photograph: Conservation Regulator Victoria Victoria Man fined after 700 frozen and taxidermied animals found on Victorian property Antiques store owner, 74, pleads guilty to 13 charges after regulator uncovers hundreds of animals at his home and shop Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast Jordyn Beazley Wed 21 Oct 2026 22.24 EDT Last modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 22.32 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The white-walled room packed with magpies, galahs and sulphur-crested cockatoos, foxes and possums is eerily quiet. As a video pans across shelves filled with these and many other species, there is no flapping or squawking or hissing; the animals are frozen and silent. They are among the more than 700 native animals that were found illegally taxidermied and frozen that were seized from the property of a Victorian antiques store owner last year. On Tuesday, 74-year-old Glenn Richard Rollo was fined $10,000 by a court after he pleaded guilty to 13 charges, including selling and possessing protected and threatened wildlife and failing to provide treatment to a sick animal. View image in fullscreen An emu at the Kyneton property. Photograph: Conservation Regulator Victoria The regulator searched his property as part of a broader crackdown on the illegal wildlife trade, executing search warrants for the man’s store and home in April last year. Restrictions on selling and possessing threatened and protected species apply to both living and dead animals. During their search they found 14 freezers containing animals. Across the property they found hundreds of dead reptiles, native birds and mammals, including 78 emus, 42 brushtail possums and 26 echidnas. They also found the remains of threatened species, including the barking owl, diamond python and Murray River short-necked turtle. In addition to the dead animals, 15 live reptiles were found in enclosures, including North American red-eared slider turtles and corn snakes. Six of the reptiles, the regulator said, were not being kept under the required animal welfare standards. The regulator said the man did not have the licence of authorisation under Victoria’s wildlife laws to obtain or possess the animals. Wildlife in Victoria is protected under the Wildlife Act 1975, which outlaws taking native animals without approval. A commercial wildlife licence or private wildlife licence is required to trade dead animals. Victorians who wish to taxidermy animals are also required obtain a licence under the conservation regulator. During an appearance before Kynton local court on Tuesday, magistrate Patrick Southey reportedly told the man: “It is bewildering that a man of your intelligence and knowledge and love of wildlife would arrogantly flout the law so comprehensively.” View image in fullscreen An image taken at the Victorian antiques store owner’s property. Photograph: Conservation Regulator Victoria The conservation regulator director of regulatory operations, Cal Heppell, said: “The scale of offending in this case highlights why Victoria has strong protections in place for wildlife and animal welfare. “Our laws and permit systems help protect wildlife from unlawful exploitation, ensure animals are appropriately cared for and safeguard Victoria’s environment and biodiversity from potential threats. “These requirements are not optional. Anyone who keeps, trades or possesses wildlife must comply with the law.” Victoria Animal Justice party MP Georgie Purcell said the wildlife laws in Victoria are not strong enough and called on the government to modernise the 50-year-old welfare act. “This is a horrific case that has rattled our community of Kyneton but it should serve as a wake-up call as to just how broken our so-called wildlife protection laws are here in Victoria,” she said. Purcell said that the $10,000 fine for possessing 700 dead native animals and keeping reptiles in poor conditions was “barely a deterrent and doesn’t send a message to the community that wildlife are respected and protected in Victoria”. “The government talks a big game about protecting wildlife but cases like this show just how badly our native animals are being let down. If hundreds of native animals can end up dead in someone’s collection, questions need to be asked why the government has continued to stall when it comes to ensuring these laws meet community expectations.” Explore more on these topics Victoria news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://breakingdefense.com/2026/10/poli.text: Panellists at the Warsaw Security Forum discussion European military plans (Warsaw Security Forum) WARSAW — Poland’s national defense minister is calling on Europe to develop an “enduring, predictable” alliance with the US, encompassing information exchange, military capabilities and defense industry collaboration. “I believe that within the ‘NATO 3.0’ strategy, it is worth emphasizing a strategy for the defense industry,” Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz told the Warsaw Security Conference on Monday. “Relocating production lines and maintenance facilities to Europe, for instance, for Patriot missiles and systems, is crucial for the independence of both the United States and Europe.” The comments arrived on the same day that Polish army operational commander Gen. Ireneusz Nowak noted at the event that Patriot deliveries are set to be held up . “At this point it looks like we are going to be affected as well,” he said. “That’s very visible in the area of PAC-3 MSE Patriot missiles, they’re going to be delayed for sure .” Ukraine has called on European partners to supply it with additional Patriot missiles to fend off Russian attacks. Kosiniak-Kamysz said the current situation in Ukraine shows how dangerous a breakdown in supply chains would be in a crisis scenario, so Europe must do everything to be strong and independent enough to take action toward greater reindustrialization. Additionally, he warned that the European Union has been grappling with the issue of military mobility for years, and “yet, there are still no decisions in place to allow for the free movement of our troops without requiring the consent of individual regions.” The matter needs to be resolved as soon as possible, he stressed, through the adoption of sound legislation. “It should be automatic: if someone calls for help, they want those troops to reach them, and everyone else should provide support,” he explained. From a big picture perspective, Europe cannot wait until 2035 to become strong, said Kosiniak-Kamysz, as he argued that NATO’s 5 percent GDP defense spending pledge should be brought forward to 2030. Kosiniak-Kamysz said Europe must make its defense industry supply chains independent, and this is a task that needs to be addressed as a matter of urgency, because “we cannot rule out equipment from outside the European Union if it is critically needed.” In his view, it stands to reason that collaboration with the US on items like low-cost, long-range precision strike capabilities, drones and anti-drone systems, as well as artificial intelligence, could prove worthwhile. “So let us not rule out the possibility of creating Polish-US or European-US joint ventures, that could also tap into [SAFE] European funds,” he said. Of the €44 billion ($49 billion) from the SAFE program, nearly one-third went to Poland, and two-thirds of that amount has already been allocated to the Polish defense industry. At a strategic level, he also declared that Poland is stronger with Washington’s backing. “The more American troops there are in Poland, and if we have a permanent base and a lasting American military presence, the better equipped we are to shoulder responsibility for NATO’s eastern flank,” he said. Kosiniak-Kamysz said also Warsaw will be ready for full-scale deterrence, thanks to investments in the defense industry, military mobility, transatlantic cooperation, relocating production to Europe, and joint investments in critical defense capabilities. Speaking alongside Kosiniak-Kamysz, Minister of National Defence of Lithuania Robertas Kaunas said in the case of a Russian attack against Lithuania, it might be two weeks before US, Polish, German, British troops could arrive and reach the Soviet border to Lithuania. He echoed Kosiniak-Kamysz words, saying his country is investing in a national division, and an anti-drone air defense system, combining all different types of sensors, under a single ecosystem, backed by artificial intelligence. Elsewhere, NATO Deputy Secretary General Radmila Shekerinska said that different things required to implement the alliance’s newly unveiled “ theory of victory ,” includes logistics, procurement and intelligence. “NATO is able to defend us. … But in order for all of us to keep this strategic advantage that we have [to] invest, create the capabilities, apply them, employ them, train the troops,” she said. Shekerinska said NATO needs to speed up procurement procedures “to prepare [a] completely new approach in what is the capability, and how to make sure that NATO will have them when it will be needed.” Rounding off panelist contributions, Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka, Poland’s Secretary of State for Defense, said she hopes the moment has come for the US government and US companies to finally agree on co-production in Europe, as US warehouses are empty. According to her, Warsaw is open to other countries, setting up shop in Poland for maintenance, logistics or production. “If there’s any foreign company trying to sell something to us, we are not only looking on the quality and price, we give four extra conditions: the maintenance center, co-production, local suppliers or at least investing in education here,” Sobkowiak-Czarnecka stressed. She added that the issue of standing up local maintenance centers is one the Polish government is trying to resolve with from Washington. “We are open for co-production, we are open … [to] companies from different parts of the world, but the condition is you have to work with our industry,” she concluded.
